slides.title: What is an Iterator?

blocks.text: An iterator is an object that allows the user to loop through the elements of a collection.
It works with a collection but is defined as a separate object.
Iterators are used in the Java collection classes, such as
ArrayList and LinkedList.
They simplify the classic step of accessing and processing the elements in a collection.
We will use the iterator concept to define our own iterators.

slides.title: The Iterable Interface

blocks.text: Java implements iterators using two generic interfaces for a collection of elements: Iterable<T> and Iterator<T>.
The Iterable interface has only one method: iterator()
Method Description
Iterator<T> iterator()
Returns an iterator object for a collection
The iterator() method returns an object, which is used to iterate over a collection of elements.
A collection is iterable if it implements the iterator() method in the Iterable interface.

slides.title: The Iterator Interface

blocks.text: The generic Iterator<T> interface contains three methods:
hasNext(), next(), and remove().
The hasNext() and next() methods can be used together to loop through and access all the elements of a collection.
The remove() method deletes the current element of a collection, when it is accessed.
Method Description

Boolean hasNext()
T next()
void remove()
Returns true if the collection has more elements
Returns the next element in the collection
Removes the current element from the collection

slides.title: Using the for-each Loop

blocks.text: Way-3: use the for-each loop to traverse the list
Internally, the for-each loop uses an iterator. It can be used on any collection that implements the Iterable interface.
However, cannot use this approach to remove elements.

slides.title: When to use an Iterator object

blocks.text: You may want to use an Iterator object explicitly if you don't want to process all the elements.
For example, searching for a particular element
You may also want to use an Iterator object if you want to call the remove method to remove some elements.
The for-each loop does not give access to remove method.
If a class does not implement the Iterable interface, then the Iterator object and the for-each loop cannot be used to traverse the elements of the collection.

slides.title: Using an Iterator to Remove Elements

blocks.text: Using an iterator object is more efficient when traversing and removing specific elements from a list.
For example, we can search for all occurrences of a specific element and remove them from the list.

slides.title: Other Iterator Issues

blocks.text: There is no assumption about the order in which an
Iterator object delivers the elements of a collection.
In the case of a list, there is a linear order, so the iterator typically follows this order.
The structure of the underlying collection should not be changed while an iterator is being used.
Most iterators in the Java API are fail-fast, meaning they
throw the ConcurrentModificationException if an
element is added while the iterator is being used.

slides.title: Implementing an Array List Iterator

blocks.text: Our ArrayList class does not implement the Iterable interface and does not provide an iterator() method.
We cannot use the for-each loop to iterate over the elements.
To have this capability, our revised ArrayList implements the Iterable interface and the iterator() method.

slides.title: The Array List Iterator class

blocks.text: To have an iterator object, our revised ArrayList class must have a class that implements the Iterator interface.
We will name this class ArrayListIterator. It is defined as an inner private class because it is used only by the iterator() method in the outer class ArrayList.

slides.title: Nested Static Class versus Inner Class

blocks.text: Nested Static Class Inner Class (Non-Static)
Declared with the static modifier Declared without the static modifier
It can only access the static members of the outer class.
It has access to ALL the members of the outer class, including private members.
It can be instantiated without creating an instance of the outer class.
It cannot be instantiated without creating an instance of the outer class.
When a nested static class object is created, it exists on its own and does not require any outer class object.
When an inner class object is created, it references the outer class object and has access to all its members.
Typically used as a helper class that logically groups with the outer class.
Typically used when the inner class needs access to all the members of the outer class.
For example, Node<T> is a nested static class under the LinkedList<T> class.
For example, ArrayListIterator is an inner class under the ArrayList<T> class.

slides.title: Counting the Modifications

blocks.text: The outer class ArrayList should count the modifications done on a list object by the add and remove methods.
modCount counts all the modifications done by the add and remove methods. It is checked by an iterator to ensure that no changes are done to a list while an iterator is used.

blocks.text: The add and remove methods should increment the modCount variable indicating that the list is modified.
